staged_snapshot.description_long: In June 2025, federal immigration agents conducted workplace enforcement operations in Los Angeles, including raids at a clothing manufacturer and other worksites. The actions drew protests and became part of a wider dispute over the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement. Contemporary reporting described arrests and the presence of federal agents at work locations; it did not establish the original entry’s broader account of a nationwide mandatory E-Verify expansion, routine warrantless arrests anywhere in the country, or a coordinated seven-day schedule designed to meet arrest quotas. Employer guidance supplied with the entry also distinguishes entry into public areas from searches of private areas, for which it says a judicial warrant or consent is generally required. The supported event is therefore the Los Angeles workplace enforcement, with its location and date made explicit. The broader claims about legal authority, E-Verify, worker retaliation, surveillance mapping, and national scope should not be attached to this event without additional records. The cited reporting documents enforcement actions, not every claimed motive or downstream effect.

Contemporary reporting and government materials describe the transaction as a loan to the casino during a period of financial pressure. New Jersey gaming authorities determined that the chip purchase violated state gaming laws, and Trump Castle agreed to a civil penalty. The episode can therefore be described as a regulatory violation involving a loan to the casino. The evidence does not support treating the transaction as a direct transfer of cash to Donald Trump personally, nor does the supplied material establish every detail of the original title’s account of money moving “to Donald.” The complaint and reporting concern the casino transaction and its legal treatment. This narrower account preserves the documented connection to Fred Trump and Trump Castle while distinguishing the casino’s receipt of funds from a personal transfer to its owner. The original title and categorization should be revised to reflect the supported legal finding rather than an imprecise beneficiary claim.

staged_snapshot.title: Ivanka Trump Testifies in DC Inquiry into Inaugural Committee Spending
staged_snapshot.description_short: Ivanka Trump Testifies in DC Inquiry into Inaugural Committee Spending
staged_snapshot.description_medium: On December 1, 2020, Ivanka Trump sat for a deposition with the D.C. attorney general’s office during its investigation into the 2017 Trump Presidential Inaugural Committee. ABC News reported that the inquiry examined committee spending at the Trump International Hotel. Her lawyer said she connected the parties and told the hotel to charge a fair-market rate. The report describes investigative allegations and testimony; it identifies no knowingly false answer or finding of perjury. The original title’s claim that she lied under oath is unsupported and is omitted.
staged_snapshot.description_long: On December 1, 2020, Ivanka Trump gave a deposition to the Washington, D.C., attorney general’s office during its investigation of the Trump 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee. ABC News reported that investigators were examining committee spending, including payments for event space at the Trump International Hotel in Washington. The D.C. attorney general’s filing compared a $5,000 charge for a prayer breakfast using the venue earlier on Inauguration Day with the committee’s later $175,000 payment for the same event space. Ivanka Trump’s lawyer told ABC that her role was limited to connecting the parties and instructing the hotel to charge a fair-market rate. These are reported investigative allegations and an attorney’s characterization of her role, not a judicial finding about her conduct. The available report confirms the deposition but does not quote an answer proved knowingly false, describe a perjury charge, or report a perjury finding. The supported event is her testimony in the civil inquiry. The accusation in the former title is not established by the sources and must not be presented as fact.
notes: The AP report confirms Ivanka Trump’s deposition and describes the lawsuit’s allegations about inaugural-committee payments, but identifies no knowingly false answer or perjury finding. The title’s central accusation remains unsupported.

staged_snapshot.description_long: At a June 26, 2025, meeting of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), Lyn Redwood presented claims about the vaccine preservative thimerosal. CNN and NBC News identified Redwood as a former president of Children’s Health Defense, an organization founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. CNN reported that her presentation argued thimerosal was linked to autism and other harms and appeared to cite a study that reporters could not locate. CDC scientists publicly pushed back on presentations questioning vaccine safety at the same meeting. Those details describe what was presented and reported; they do not show that the committee or CDC adopted the claims. Separate CNN and CBS reporting said HHS had hired Redwood for work connected to CDC vaccine safety, but did not establish a formal public job title. The sources support a specific account of her hiring as reported and presentation to ACIP, with attribution and limits. They do not support the original title’s insult or its assertion that she had been appointed to a specifically named vaccine-safety office. This draft describes the meeting and staffing facts without adopting an evaluative label.

staged_snapshot.description_medium: On May 22, 2026, CBS News reported that the Trump administration was preparing for possible renewed military strikes against Iran, citing sources with direct knowledge of planning. The report said diplomacy was continuing and no final decision had been made. Reuters separately reported Trump’s May 19 statement that the U.S. might strike again. These accounts describe consideration and preparation, not an order or completed strike.
staged_snapshot.description_long: On May 22, 2026, CBS News reported that the Trump administration was preparing for a possible new round of military strikes against Iran while diplomatic talks continued. The report attributed the information to sources with direct knowledge of the planning and said no final decision to strike had been made. Three days earlier, Reuters reported that President Donald Trump said the United States might need to hit Iran again and that he had been an hour away from deciding on a strike before postponing it; he said another attack could follow within days if no agreement was reached. A New York Times report published May 22 described potential target categories, including energy facilities, an underground nuclear-storage site at Isfahan, and missile sites, if Trump chose to resume attacks. These are reports about options and preparations at that time. They do not establish that Trump issued a strike order or that the specific targets were attacked. The entry is framed as reported consideration, not as a completed military action.

staged_snapshot.title: DOJ Filed 31 Suits Seeking Unredacted Voter Registration Data

preserved_fields.description_long: By April 2026, internal DOJ communications obtained by CNN revealed the Trump administration had been working for nearly a year on a covert plan to use DHS's SAVE citizenship database to identify and remove noncitizens from voter rolls, while hiding the plan's details from courts and Democratic election officials. The DOJ had brought lawsuits against the election chiefs of 31 states — primarily Democratic — demanding unredacted voter registration data including Social Security numbers, arguing noncompliance violated federal law. By July 2026, AP News reported the administration was threatening to withhold federal funding from states and warning state election officials they faced arrest if they did not remove voters flagged by the federal system — despite multiple courts having rejected the efforts as based on 'untrue claims about widespread voting fraud.' At least 67 million voter registrations had been run through federal databases with tens of thousands flagged, including documented cases of U.S. citizens wrongly identified by the SAVE system.

staged_snapshot.description_short: The 2025 reconciliation law ended certain IRA wind and solar electricity credits for covered facilities placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027.
staged_snapshot.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, amended the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-electricity production and investment credits. For covered wind and solar facilities, the law ends Sections 45Y and 48E credits for facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, subject to statutory rules. It did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit.
staged_snapshot.description_long: President Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the Internal Revenue Code’s clean-electricity production credit under Section 45Y and clean-electricity investment credit under Section 48E. The statute provides that these credits do not apply to covered wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, and includes separate transition rules concerning when construction begins. The change narrows the period in which some Inflation Reduction Act clean-electricity credits can be claimed; it is more precise to describe it as a statutory termination for covered facilities than as blanket rescission of all IRA tax credits. Reuters’ July 2025 reporting described broader investment uncertainty after subsidy changes, but the statute is the stronger source for which credits and facilities are affected. The supplied row does not identify a credit-by-credit inventory, and this draft does not claim that all solar, wind, battery, electric-vehicle or already-committed projects lost support. The legal text establishes the cutoff and scope; project-specific eligibility depends on statutory definitions and transition provisions.

This correction focuses on the later dinner and its qualification mechanism, the event covered by the linked Reuters article. It does not use that May report to support the separate January launch claim about anonymous foreign wallets or an SEC decision.
